summary: Round 2's two majors are fixed in the paragraphs that state them, and I verified the tree facts the fixes rest on: Checkpoint.decode really is a strict equality check (format/src/main/java/binjava/format/Checkpoint.java:151) and CheckpointCursor really does gloss IOException as 'the store is unreachable' (CheckpointCursor.java:67); CheckpointTest asserts <64 KiB at 1,600 streams (CheckpointTest.java:153-169); ADR-0031 is now a precondition rather than an argument; the per-SegmentCommit placement and the per-ingester minting site are both correct and the M4-invisibility claim behind the first one holds against this tree -- DefaultIngest.flushLocked calls sequencer.commit under the ingest lock (DefaultIngest.java:338-349) and BatchingSequencer is constructed in no production path, so a multi-segment delta needs a second caller, which is M5. That is a property of today's wiring rather than of commitAll, and it is worth saying so in the ADR. Cost checks out: detection is in-memory, answering is one GET per replay, the checkpoint grows in SIZE per pod and adds no request that scales with pods, shards or indices. What does not hold together is where the R2a fix landed and how far it reaches. The pointer appears in exactly one Consequences paragraph and in NONE of the three places that say what gets encoded -- the ADR's own 'Which formats change' bullet, the ADR-0033 amendment banner, and M4.10c's row, all three of which still say the slot is (incarnationId, lastAppliedFlushSeq). And with one pointer per pod, answering reaches only the pod's NEWEST flushSeq while detection reaches every earlier one, which is R2a's asymmetry one step in and is a case the Decision section names explicitly. Separately, the archive row this commit adds contradicts the decision's own load-bearing minting clause using the exact noun the ADR calls wrong. On the staged rounds:M4.10b entry: its claims check out -- the round-1 measurement, the dropped pointer, the two M4-invisible shapes, 'Filed as M4.46' (the row is added by this commit), and it correctly says 'per INGESTER PROCESS', which is what makes finding R3c a contradiction inside one commit rather than a difference of opinion. Its split argument covers the ADR but not the M4.46 row and notes section it also carries; that is disclosed in the entry rather than silent, so I raise it as an observation, not a finding.

findings.summary: THE R2a FIX LANDED IN THE ONE SECTION NOBODY ENCODES FROM. Consequences now says 'The slot carries a POINTER beside the watermark, (epoch, sequence) of the delta that last applied for that pod'. The section titled 'Which formats change' still says '`pods` becomes `podId -> (incarnationId, lastAppliedFlushSeq)`' -- a pair, no pointer. So does the ADR-0033 amendment banner added by this same commit ('gains an `incarnationId` beside it', 0033-...md:6-10), and so does M4.10c's rewritten row, which is the spec the implementing session will build from ('`Checkpoint.pods` becomes `podId -> (incarnationId, lastAppliedFlushSeq)`', backlog.md:123). Three normative statements against one Consequences paragraph.
findings.failure_scenario: A session picks M4.10c. Its row is the task, and the row names ADR-0036, so the session reads the ADR's 'Which formats change' section -- the section whose title answers the question it was given. Both say a pair. It encodes (incarnationId, lastAppliedFlushSeq), writes the new golden, bumps the version, and every gate goes green because the encoder, the decoder, the fake and the golden all agree with each other and with the row. M4.10d then lands the dedup and discovers that a detected replay has nothing durable leading back to its offsets below the newest checkpoint -- exactly the defect R2a raised, shipped in the format, with the fix sitting in a paragraph that describes a consequence of a field the format does not carry. Two accepted ADRs and one open row then disagree about what Checkpoint.pods contains, which is the same shape as this task's earlier F2.
findings.suggestion: State the slot once, in 'Which formats change': `podId -> (incarnationId, lastAppliedFlushSeq, epoch, sequence)`, and make the Consequences paragraph explain it rather than introduce it. Propagate the same shape into M4.10c's row and the ADR-0033 banner -- or, if the pointer is deliberately not stored, delete the paragraph and say what answers a replay instead.

findings.summary: 'ONE GET ANSWERS THE REPLAY' IS TRUE ONLY FOR THE NEWEST flushSeq PER POD, AND THE DECISION SECTION NAMES THE OTHER CASE ITSELF. The slot holds ONE pointer, 'the delta that LAST applied for that pod'. Detection is unbounded-depth by construction (`flushSeq <= lastAppliedFlushSeq`), and the Decision explicitly contemplates a replay strictly below the watermark: 'A batch may carry several requests from one pod -- commitAll is the primitive -- and `<=` handles a replay of the lower of them.' For any such replay the pointer names the wrong delta. So answering is watermark-bounded while detection is not -- the R2a asymmetry moved one step in rather than removed -- and the rejection of 'bound the window to the uncheckpointed tail' ('neither detected nor answered') claims a property this design does not have for flushSeq < lastApplied.
findings.failure_scenario: Pod `poda`, incarnation I, commits flushSeq 4 then 5. The slot holds lastApplied=5 and the pointer to flush 5's delta. A duplicate of flushSeq 4 arrives -- the case the Decision names. Detection fires correctly. M4.10d's row, rewritten by this commit, says a replay is 'answered with the ORIGINAL offsets' with no bound on which, and the only durable lead is the pointer. The implementer GETs the delta it names and returns flush 5's segmentKey and firstOffset for flush 4's records: a caller acked at offsets that resolve to another flush's records, which is precisely the invariant M4.46's reframing in this same commit exists to name ('a committed offset must resolve to the records committed at it'). The alternative -- return nothing -- silently contradicts M4.10b's own stated property that a replay must be ANSWERED, not merely detected, and no test in M4.10d would be written to catch either, because the ADR says answering costs one GET and stops.
findings.suggestion: State the bound as part of the decision, not as an aside: answering is exact for the most recent flushSeq per (podId, incarnationId), and a detected replay of an earlier flushSeq is refused WITHOUT offsets (or however it is to be handled), with one sentence on why that is acceptable. Then soften the 'neither detected nor answered' rejection of the tail alternative so it does not claim reach the chosen design lacks, and give M4.10d's row the same bound so its acceptance criterion is writable.

findings.summary: THE ARCHIVE ROW THIS COMMIT ADDS CONTRADICTS THE DECISION'S OWN LOAD-BEARING CLAUSE, USING THE NOUN THE ADR CALLS WRONG. The ADR: 'incarnationId is minted once per INGESTER process -- the same object that mints flushSeq' and '⚠️ THE MINTING SITE IS PART OF THE DECISION ... The producer is the record supplier (glossary.md), and is the wrong noun'. The M4.10b row landed in backlog-done.md by the same commit: 'with the incarnation minted per producer process'. The commit's own baselines/review.txt entry gets it right ('per INGESTER PROCESS'), so the fact is correct in two copies of three -- the duplicate-fact failure rounds:M4.10a records about itself.
findings.failure_scenario: backlog-done.md is the summary a session reads when it does not load the ADR: M4.15 writing M4's VERIFIED.md, or a session grepping the archive to learn what M4.10b decided before picking M4.10d. It reads 'minted per producer process'. Per glossary.md a producer is whatever supplies records -- a remote client POSTing _bulk -- so the row says the id belongs to the record supplier rather than to the ingester process that holds flushSeq. Implemented that way there is no id tied to the DefaultIngest incarnation at all, dedup keys on something the restarting process does not own, and the restart the whole ADR exists to discriminate is discriminated by nothing -- while every sequencer-seam test passes, because those tests supply the incarnation, which is the mutation the ADR itself names.
findings.suggestion: One word in the archive row: 'minted per ingester process'.

findings.summary: THE 175/200 FIGURE IS CORRECTED IN ONE OF THREE COPIES. M4.46's notes, added by this commit, say the 175/200 on Clock.systemUTC() 'is an artifact of a fixture whose appends fall inside one millisecond, NOT an 87% production rate'. The ADR's Context still quotes '175/200 under Clock.systemUTC() in the standard fixture' with no such caveat, and the archive row says '175/200 on the real clock' -- which reads as a real-clock rate and is the reading the notes were reframed to prevent.
findings.failure_scenario: A later session, or an M4.46 implementer, quotes an accepted ADR for an 87% collision rate under the real clock, sizes the fix or its urgency against that number, and is wrong by roughly the whole figure. The decision itself is unaffected -- it rests on the frozen/regressed clock, which is measured and sound -- so this is severity minor, but it is a measured number whose scope is misstated in the durable record.
findings.suggestion: Carry the notes' caveat into the ADR Context sentence and drop 'on the real clock' from the archive row, or drop the 175/200 from both and keep only 200/200 frozen, which is what the argument uses.

findings.summary: THE SIZE PARAGRAPH ADDS A FIELD AND KEEPS THE OLD NUMBER. It now reads 'grows by fixed-width fields per pod. An incarnationId is 16 bytes as a UUID and the pointer is two longs' and then concludes with the unchanged '16 bytes per pod does not approach the remainder'. With the pointer the per-pod cost is 32 bytes, not 16.
findings.failure_scenario: The remainder under the 64 KiB assertion is about 26 KiB, so the conclusion is unchanged but the pod headroom the sentence implies is halved -- roughly 1,600 pods at 16 bytes, roughly 800 at 32, before the podId strings the map already stores. Someone sizing a large fleet against this paragraph takes the wrong figure from the sentence that carries a number rather than from the one that lists the fields, in an ADR whose own skill says an argument without its number is an assertion.
findings.suggestion: Say 32 bytes per pod in the concluding clause and, if the headroom is the point, quote the pod count it buys.
